title: Pir Budhu Shah
hookLine: a Sufi who sent his sons and followers to fight beside the Guru at Bhangani, where two sons fell

cards: A recommendation can be a heavy thing to give. You put your name next to someone else's, and if they let the other person down, part of that is on you. Now raise the stakes.
A holy man of one faith vouches for a band of soldiers to a teacher of another faith. The soldiers take the pay. Then, on the eve of a battle, most of them walk away.
The holy man could send an apology. He could stay home. Instead, tradition says, he gathers his own sons and his own followers and rides toward the fighting.

teach.b: Pir Budhu Shah was a Sufi, a Muslim teacher of the inner path, who lived at Sadhaura, not far from where the young Guru Gobind Singh was staying in the hills. Pir is a title for a spiritual guide.

teach.h: THE SOLDIERS HE VOUCHED FOR LEFT.
teach.b: Tradition says the two men met and respected each other, and that the Pir recommended a company of Pathan soldiers who needed work. The Guru took them on.
Then came Bhangani, the battle where hill rajas marched against him. Tradition says most of those Pathans deserted before the fighting, and only a few stayed. The Pir did not send excuses.
He came himself, with his sons and his followers, to stand beside the Guru. And in that fighting, tradition says, two of his sons were killed.
A father of one faith lost two sons defending a teacher of another, because, the story says, his word had been given. Afterward, the story goes, the Guru wanted to honor him.

teach.h: HE ASKED ONLY FOR A COMB.
teach.b: Tradition says the Pir asked for the comb the Guru had just used, with strands of his hair still caught in it, and the Guru gave it to him, along with a turban. Not land, not gold: just a comb.
Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah with love.
His story is told when people ask what friendship between faiths can look like. Not a polite handshake. Keeping your word when it costs you, beside someone who prays differently.
And it reminds Sikhs that among the people around the Gurus were Muslims who gave everything.

how: Sikhs remember Pir Budhu Shah in tellings of the battle of Bhangani and in talks and kirtan programs about the Muslims who stood with the Gurus, and his town of Sadhaura is remembered in that story.

the soldiers he recommended all stayed to fight
tradition says most of them deserted before the battle, so he came himself.
afterward, tradition says, he asked the Guru for a comb
not land or gold: the comb the Guru had just used, with strands of hair in it.

games.q: you're Pir Budhu Shah. the soldiers you vouched for to the Guru have deserted on the eve of battle. what do you do?
o: send a message of apology and stay home.
ride in with your own sons and followers.
tell the Guru they were never your responsibility.
games.why: tradition says he came himself with his sons and followers, and two of his sons fell at Bhangani.

practice: Bring to mind someone outside your own circle, another faith, another background, even a stranger, who once gave something up for you or for people you love. Let yourself remember what it cost them.
If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer.
